responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character48_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
You know, for Character48_F, “fairness” wasn’t some abstract idea you read about in a textbook. It was real, like the kind of thing she’d notice standing in line at the unemployment office or waiting for her paycheck to clear so she could pay the electric bill. She always said fairness meant everybody getting a shot—not handouts, but a *chance*. Like, if you’re working hard, showing up on time, trying to do right by your kids, then you shouldn’t get pushed aside just because someone else’s got connections or money.

She used to talk about how frustrating it was when people assumed she didn’t care about others just because she worried about her own family making it. That wasn’t selfish, she’d say—it was survival. Fairness, to her, meant rules that didn’t favor the rich or punish the poor for things they couldn’t control—like where you were born, who your parents were, or whether your town lost its factory jobs to places overseas.

As for “belonging,” that hit close to home. She grew up in a small Rust Belt town where folks knew each other’s grandparents. But over the years, people moved away, factories shut down, and it felt like the community was fading. She missed that feeling of being *known*—not famous, just… seen. Like when the diner waitress remembered how you took your coffee, or your neighbor shoveled your walk without being asked.

She believed belonging wasn’t automatic. You had to earn it by showing up—by helping out after a storm, keeping your yard clean, respecting the neighborhood. And she thought newcomers should be willing to do that too—not to erase where they came from, but to become part of something new together. She wasn’t against change, but she wanted it to feel mutual, not one-sided.

And “community”? That was sacred to her. Not perfect—she knew her town had its share of drunks, gossipers, people who judged too quick—but still, it mattered. A real community looked out for its own. She remembered when her brother got hurt on the job and couldn’t work for months—how neighbors brought meals, church folks sent cards, even the guy from the corner store let her charge milk until payday. That kind of thing shaped her.

So when we talked about immigration, it wasn’t just politics. It was: *Can this person be part of that web? Will they help hold it up, or will the weight break what little’s left?* She didn’t hate strangers. But she feared losing what little stability she had—and watching others bypass the line she’d waited in her whole life.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character48_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*[Sitting back slightly, hands resting on knees, voice steady but thoughtful]*

You know, I’ll be honest—I sit here in this garden, pulling weeds out of the tomato bed, and sometimes I feel like I’m in a whole different world than the one I grew up in. Back then, most folks looked like me, talked like me, went to the same church or their kids played Little League together. Now? I hear Spanish, Arabic, Vietnamese—sometimes all before lunch. Kids running around with hijabs or dreads or clothes I’ve never seen before. And not everyone’s got a job. Some are struggling. Some are just… trying.

I don’t mind the differences, not really. What bothers me is when it feels like no one’s connecting. Like we’re all living side by side but not *with* each other. I once brought extra zucchini over to that young couple from Somalia who moved into Mrs. Callahan’s old place—their garden was all weeds, and I thought, *maybe they don’t know how to start.* But the woman just looked scared, shut the door quick. Maybe she didn’t understand. Maybe she thought I was judging her. That stung.

But then there’s Mr. Tran down at plot seven—he’s from Vietnam, been here thirty years—and he’ll hand me okra without a word, just a nod. We don’t talk much, but we know each other now. Or Leticia, from Guatemala, runs the little daycare out of her home. Her kids help water the marigolds here every morning. She smiles, says good morning, asks about my arthritis. That feels real.

What gets hard is when people are dealing with things—alcohol, drugs, sickness—and it spills into the shared space. Last summer, that guy in Unit B was yelling every night, drunk off his feet, scaring the kids. Landlord did nothing for weeks. Then someone said he was a refugee, had “trauma,” so we were supposed to just tolerate it? I get trauma. My daddy came back from ‘Nam half gone. But we didn’t yell at neighbors or leave trash everywhere. We *managed*, because that’s what you do if you want to belong.

And yeah, I see folks with rainbow flags, unmarried couples raising kids together, grandmas doing the parenting again. At first, it made me uncomfortable—raised Catholic, you know how it is—but then I watched them care for each other. Saw that single dad from Honduras cry when his son got accepted to college. Watched two women raise three foster kids like they were born to it.

So my feelings? Mixed. I want to welcome people. I really do. But I need to see that they *want* to be part of this place—not just live in it, but care about it. Tend the garden, pick up the litter, keep their voices down at night. That’s how trust grows. Not with speeches or slogans, but with showing up. Like Mr. Tran with his okra. Like Leticia’s kids watering flowers.

That’s belonging, to me. Not everyone the same. Just everyone trying.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*[Leans forward a bit, wiping her hands on an old rag, voice lower now—more personal]*

Look… I’ve lived long enough to know nobody’s perfect. We’ve all got something. My cousin’s been in and out of rehab since the ‘90s. My sister’s partner—they’re not married, live together with their two boys—used to make *me* uncomfortable at first. Felt like they were thumbing their nose at tradition. But then I saw how hard they work, how they fight for their kids’ school programs, how he fixed my fence when the storm blew it over. Changed my mind real quick.

So yeah—unconventional lifestyles? They’re just… lives. Some people drink too much—that’s been true forever. I remember my uncle disappearing for days during binges. Wasn’t right, but we didn’t kick him out of family dinners. We kept the door open. Same with folks struggling with drugs now. I don’t want needles in the playground, Lord no—but I also don’t think locking them up or shunning them helps. What helps is if someone *talks* to them. Like that outreach worker from the clinic who goes around handing out clean kits and actually *knows* people by name. She says half the battle is being seen.

And infectious diseases—well, after what we lived through with HIV back in the day, and then the hepatitis scare at the plant—I learned real fast that fear doesn’t protect you. Ignorance does more harm than germs. One of my coworkers got laid off because people thought he was “dangerous” just ’cause he was sick. That wasn’t fair. That was panic. So yeah, special care and understanding matter—not just for kindness, but because we’re all safer when people aren’t afraid to come forward.

Now, different backgrounds—race, religion, language—that’s where I’ll admit I had to grow. I won’t lie. When the mosque went up on 5th Street, I believed some ugly things I heard. Then I met Amina, whose son goes to school with my grandson. Sweetest kid, always brings me dates during Ramadan now. And she asked me once, plain as day: *“Do you think we want to be here if we didn’t have to?”* Broke my heart a little.

Same with same-sex couples. I used to say it wasn’t “natural.” But then Pastor Dan’s daughter came out, and he still preached every Sunday, still shook everyone’s hand after service. Said love was love when it lifted people up. Made me rethink a lot.

What makes people feel comfortable? It ain’t grand gestures. It’s small things. Saying hello. Not crossing the street when someone looks different. Letting your kid play with theirs. Asking someone’s name instead of assuming. Tolerance? Yeah, we need more of it—but only if it comes with honesty. Because tolerance can be cold. Like, “I’ll let you exist, but I don’t care about you.” I want something warmer. *Curiosity*, maybe. Like, “Tell me about your food. Why do you celebrate that holiday? Can I bring something to the potluck?”

Communication breaks walls. Silence builds them.

Are there situations where it’s harder? Of course. When someone’s drunk and aggressive, or when families move in six to a one-bedroom apartment and trash piles up—then I worry about safety, about fairness to others trying to keep things decent. But even then, I ask: *What’s their story?* Maybe they fled violence. Maybe they’re waiting on aid that never comes. Doesn’t excuse everything, but it helps me pause before I judge.

We’ve all needed grace at some point. I sure have. So I try to give it—especially when the other person’s trying. That’s the line for me: Are they trying to be part of this place, or are they just using it?

Because community only works both ways. You get support, you give respect. You take care of your space, I’ll welcome you into mine.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character48_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*[Sighs, rubs her knee like it’s bothering her—same way she used to when talking about hard things over coffee]*

Fairness… when there ain’t enough to go around? That cuts deep. I’ll tell you straight: I don’t believe in keeping people out just because they’re different. But I *do* believe that if you’ve spent thirty years working the same line, coming home with grease under your nails, raising kids on two jobs, and then one day they bring in workers from somewhere else—cheaper, quieter, easier to push around—it ain’t fair. It *hurts*. Feels like your loyalty meant nothing.

When the auto plant closed, half our town got wiped out. Men my age—skilled, proud, strong—they stood in line for months. Nothing. Then they opened that warehouse out by the highway, and sure, jobs came back. But guess who got hired first? Not us. They brought in crews from other states, some undocumented, paying them less, no benefits, and said, “Well, they’re more reliable.” Reliable? Because they’re scared to speak up! Scared to say the machine’s dangerous or the hours are killing them. That ain’t reliable—that’s exploitation. And it makes locals bitter. Not because we hate immigrants, but because the system *uses* them to replace us.

So what’s fair? To me, fairness means *local folks get first shot* at the work, especially when times are tough. Not forever—just first chance. If a job opens up, run it through the unemployment office, give notice at the community center, let people here try out. Train ‘em if they need it, yeah—but don’t skip right to bringing in outsiders while your neighbors sit idle.

And if migrant workers *are* needed—say, seasonal farm work, or rebuilding after a storm, stuff nobody local can or will do—then fine. Bring ‘em in. But *legally*, with rules. Pay minimum wage. Same safety standards. No undercutting. No giving breaks to employers just because cheap labor shows up. That’s how you keep it fair—for everyone.

I remember talking to a Guatemalan guy once, picking apples up north. He told me he sent every dollar home to his mom and three kids. Broke my heart, but I respected him—he wasn’t trying to take anything. Just wanted to work. So I don’t blame *him*. I blame the bosses who’d rather hire him for less than pay me a living wage. That’s where the unfairness starts—not with the worker, but with the game being rigged.

Balance? It’s gotta be based on honesty. If we need help, let’s say so—and bring people in the right way. Not as replacements, but as helpers. And make sure they’re treated right too. Because if they’re exploited, *we’re* all worse off. Drives wages down. Breaks trust. Makes people angry at each other instead of at the ones really in charge.

Belonging shouldn’t depend on your passport. But neither should survival depend on how desperate someone is. Fairness means protecting the dignity of *all* workers—local and migrant—by making the rules tight, clear, and enforced. No backdoors. No favors.

That’s how you build something lasting. Not by pushing anyone out—but by making sure nobody gets thrown under the bus just to survive.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character48_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*[Leans back against the bench, eyes on the garden, voice quieter now—like she’s sorting things out as she speaks]*

When you hear all those voices on TV—the yelling, the slogans, the politicians pointing fingers—it gets loud real fast. But when I sit here, quiet, with dirt on my hands and the sun on my face, I try to separate what *feels* true from what actually *is*.

First—yes, immigrants fill jobs people won’t do. That part? I believe it. I’ve seen it. Who wants to gut fish at 4 a.m. in that cold plant upstate? Who’s gonna pick strawberries in July heat for ten bucks an hour? Not many locals anymore. My nephew tried it one summer—quit in three days. So if folks come here and do that work, feed us, keep prices down a little? Then yeah, they’re doing something real. Vital, even. That’s reasonable.

And the cultural stuff—music, food, festivals—I’ll admit, I didn’t used to care. Thought, “Why can’t we just stick with what we know?” But then I went to that Diwali celebration downtown last year. The lights, the dancing, kids laughing… and this old man handed me a sweet rice thing wrapped in banana leaf—said it was for good luck. Made me cry, truth be told. Not because it changed my life, but because it reminded me that joy travels. Doesn’t matter where it starts. So diversity? When it’s shared, not shoved—that brings life. I’ll give that one.

But then there’s the fear. Crime. Security. Terrorism. Now, I don’t think every brown-skinned man is dangerous—don’t believe that for a second. But I *do* remember how scared we all were after Boston. After San Bernardino. And when you hear “refugee” and then six months later someone gets caught in a plot? It shakes you. Makes you wonder: are we being safe enough?

I know the stats say immigrants commit *less* crime than native-born Americans. I’ve heard that. But numbers don’t always calm the heart. I saw what happened when that halfway house opened near the school—no, it wasn’t immigrants, but it taught me something: trust has to be *earned*, not demanded. So when people worry about security, I don’t call them racists. I call them *scared*. And fear doesn’t go away with facts alone. It goes away with time, with faces, with knowing your neighbor.

Same with social tension. That’s real too. Not because people are evil—but because when everything feels unstable—jobs gone, schools underfunded, hospitals closing—then change feels like threat. You add language barriers, different customs, new demands on services, and people get nervous. Like, “Where do *we* fit?” Especially older folks, working class folks who’ve already lost so much. We need space to talk about that without being called bigots.

Humanitarian side? That weighs heavy on me. I’m Christian—not perfect, but I try to live it. And Jesus said welcome the stranger. Period. So when I see kids in cages, or families walking thousands of miles just to ask for help, I feel shame. Real shame. No child should suffer for their parents’ choices. And if someone’s running from war, from rape, from starvation—what kind of person turns them away?

But—and this is a *but*—compassion can’t mean blindness. We can’t take everyone. No country can. So we gotta have order. Process. Not walls—walls feel cruel—but limits. Fair ones. Where people wait their turn, same as the rest of us did.

And employment fears? Yeah, those aren’t made up. Maybe overall wages don’t crash—but *in certain places*, in certain jobs? They do. I’ve seen factories hire guest workers at lower pay, no union, and then let long-time employees go. That ain’t right. And when housing gets tight, rent goes up, schools overcrowd—locals notice. They don’t always understand immigration policy, but they *feel* the squeeze.

So what needs more evidence? The crime link. I want proof, real local data, not headlines. And I want to hear from law enforcement—do cops really feel overwhelmed? Or is it media noise?

What needs dialogue? Everything. Seriously. We’ve stopped talking. We shout or scroll past. I’d love to sit down—me, a Somali refugee, a farm boss, a cop, a teacher—with coffee and just *ask*: What are you afraid of? What do you need? What are you proud of?

Because I’ve learned something: most people just want safety, dignity, a chance. Doesn’t matter where they started.

So I hold two truths at once:  
Immigrants help this country survive.  
And working people here deserve protection too.

Fairness isn’t picking sides. It’s making sure the system doesn’t play one group against the other.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character48_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*[Folds the rag slowly in her lap, voice firm but not loud—like she’s arrived at something after a long walk]*

Complete openness? No. As much as my heart might want to say yes—to just throw the gates open and let everyone come who’s hurting—I can’t. Not because I don’t care. But because *systems break*. Schools fill. Clinics overflow. Rent climbs. And when that happens, it’s the working poor—people like me—who get pushed out first. I’ve seen it. My cousin lost her apartment because an investor bought it and turned it into short-term rentals for newcomers with outside money. That ain’t justice.

Refusing all workers from other countries? Also no. That’s fear talking, not sense. We need help—on farms, in nursing homes, rebuilding after storms. My own mom’s in assisted living now, and half the staff come from the Philippines or Mexico. Without them? She’d be sitting in her chair all day, hungry, lonely. So shutting everyone out—that’s not only cruel, it’s stupid. We can’t do it alone.

So what works?

I’d go with *job-based admission*—but only if it’s tightly controlled. Bring people in for real labor shortages, not just to pay less. No more H-2A or guest worker programs that trap people in one job, scared to complain. If you’re coming to work, you get full rights. Minimum wage. Safety protections. A path—if you stay clean, pay taxes, learn English—to stay longer. Maybe even become part of us.

And couple that with *numerical limits*—not arbitrary, but based on what our towns can actually absorb. Not some number pulled from Washington with no clue what it means on the ground. Let local governments have a say. If Cleveland says, “We can take fifty refugee families this year and house them right,” then fine. But don’t dump two hundred in without schools, clinics, language support. That sets *everyone* up to fail—the newcomers and the neighbors.

And here’s what’s missing: *integration requirements*. Not assimilation—nobody should have to erase who they are—but basic things that let us live together. Learning English. Not fluency overnight, but enough to talk to your kid’s teacher, read a medicine label, ask for help. Taking a civics class—not a test, but something real, where you learn how town meetings work, what your rights *and* responsibilities are. Paying taxes. Obeying laws. That’s not asking too much. That’s how trust grows.

And for locals? We need support too. Job retraining. Better wages. Invest in *our* communities so we don’t feel replaced. Because when people feel secure, they’re more willing to welcome others. But when you’re scared every month about the electric bill, and then you see someone new getting help you never got? Resentment wins.

So balance? It’s this:  
Let people in—*when we need them*,  
With rules that protect *everyone*,  
Limits that respect our capacity,  
And expectations that build belonging—for them *and* for us.

Fairness isn’t about being soft or hard. It’s about being *honest*. Honest about our limits. Honest about our needs. Honest about our fears—and our hopes.

Because in the end? I don’t want a country that shuts its door.  
But I don’t want one that forgets its own people either.

I want a place where Mr. Tran can grow his vegetables,  
Where Amina’s son can dream big,  
Where my grandson has a good job,  
And where we all—no matter how we got here—know we belong *because we show up for each other.*

That’s the policy I’d back. Not perfect. But fair. And human.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character48_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character48_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*[Pauses a long moment. Takes off her glasses, wipes them slowly on the edge of her shirt—something she used to do when she was thinking hard. Her voice is softer now, not as Character48_F, but still close to her, like someone standing in her shadow]*

You know… I thought I knew her well. I *did* know her—her laugh, her stubbornness, how she’d cross her arms when she was about to say something sharp but true. But doing this—stepping into her words, really *speaking* them again—it made me see her more clearly than I have in years.

I realized something: she wasn’t afraid of strangers because they were different. She was afraid of being *erased*. Of working her whole life, playing by the rules, and then waking up one day to find no one remembered that effort. That pain isn’t hate. It’s grief. And it doesn’t go away just because someone tells you you’re “on the wrong side of history.”

Holding her voice today, I felt how much she *wanted* to be generous—but only if it was fair. Not handouts. Not guilt. Just recognition: *“See me too.”* That changed how I see the whole debate. It’s not really about borders or quotas. It’s about dignity. Who gets to belong—and who decides.

And honestly? It challenged me. I’ve always leaned more open, more welcoming—I believed if we just talked more, shared more, everything would work out. But sitting here as her, I saw the cost of that idealism on people like her. The real squeeze. The feeling that while we’re debating values, folks are losing homes, jobs, hope.

It didn’t change my belief that we should help those fleeing violence or poverty. But it made me understand why some feel that help comes at *their* expense. And that’s not bigotry—it’s betrayal. When the system fails everyone, then pits them against each other, of course it breeds anger.

So now I think: compassion has to include the working poor too. Not just newcomers. We can’t build belonging for some by destroying it for others.

In a way, doing this brought her back—not just her opinions, but her *heart*. She wasn’t simple. She held contradictions. Loved her country but was mad at it. Wanted to welcome people but needed to know they’d respect what was already here.

And maybe… maybe that’s where healing starts. Not with slogans. Not with silence. But with honest, messy conversations—like this one—where we let people be complex. Where we listen before we judge.

So thank you. For asking me to do this. It wasn’t just remembering her.  
It was hearing her again.  
And that… means more than you know.
